title: Online hate researcher keeps hammering X despite deportation threat
gist: The US State Department is using an immigration policy — blocked as unconstitutional by Judge Boasberg in July but now on appeal — to designate noncitizen platform-safety researchers as national security risks, with CCDH founder Imran Ahmed, a green card holder, facing removal after Judge Preska ruled federal courts lack jurisdiction to intervene pre-removal. Ahmed says officials cited his group's support for the EU's record $1 billion fine against X as grounds, and he is continuing to publish, including CCDH research behind a New York Times investigation that found 65 AI-generated and 75 known CSAM images persisting on X, plus a forthcoming report showing OpenAI safeguards failing.

themes.theme: Immigration policy weaponized against platform researchers

insights.claim: The US government is pursuing deportation of noncitizen technology researchers who monitor safety risks on major online platforms, and appealed a July ruling that blocked the enabling policy as unconstitutional.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Independent platform-safety research is the main external check producing the evidence regulators and litigants rely on — suppressing it reduces disclosure risk for large platforms.
insights.quote: The US is not backing down from its fight to deport noncitizen technology researchers who monitor safety risks on the biggest online platforms.
insights.locator: Opening paragraph

insights.claim: Secretary of State Marco Rubio framed the policy as preventing foreign nationals from manipulating digital town squares and censoring Americans, and said he stood 'ready and willing' to expand the list of targeted researchers.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: An explicitly expandable target list means the chilling effect extends well beyond named individuals to the entire noncitizen trust-and-safety workforce.
insights.locator: In his announcement of the policy, Secretary of State Marco Rubio explained

insights.claim: US District Judge James Boasberg stayed the policy after finding the government produced no evidence linking any targeted researcher to a foreign power attempting to censor Americans, and that the policy was broad enough to sweep in seemingly any noncitizen working in content moderation.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: An evidentiary vacuum at the district level is the strongest signal the policy is retaliatory rather than security-driven — relevant to how appellate courts will weigh it.
insights.locator: However, in his order siding with the Coalition for Independent Technology Research

insights.claim: Boasberg held that the prospect that a policy may later contribute to some noncitizen's removal does not transform a challenge to the policy into review of a removal order — the jurisdictional theory that could rescue such challenges.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: This distinction is the legal hinge determining whether any court can ever review these designations — the single variable to watch in the appeals.
insights.quote: the prospect that [a] policy may later contribute to some noncitizen’s removal does not transform a challenge to the policy into the review of an order of removal
insights.locator: Boasberg apparently agreed.

insights.claim: The government's appeal came two days after a separate court found it had no jurisdiction to decide a hate speech researcher's challenge, suggesting the timing was opportunistic.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: The government is sequencing filings to build on favorable jurisdictional rulings — a tactic that compounds across cases if unchallenged.
insights.locator: Last week, the US appealed that ruling

themes.theme: The jurisdictional trap in Ahmed's case

insights.claim: US District Judge Loretta Preska ruled that Congress removed courts' authority to block the government from initiating removal proceedings, so she could not grant a permanent injunction even though Imran Ahmed 'may very well have valid causes of action.'
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: A merits-sympathetic court declining jurisdiction is the worst outcome for researchers — it means unconstitutional policies can operate without review until after harm.
insights.quote: Ahmed may very well have valid causes of action
insights.locator: Ultimately, however, she ruled that Congress had removed courts' authority

insights.claim: Technology researchers read Preska's decision as suggesting federal courts can never review the legal basis for an immigration policy connected to removal proceedings, even if that policy is unconstitutional.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: If that reading holds, immigration status becomes a general-purpose, unreviewable lever against any noncitizen critic of a politically connected company.
insights.locator: Technology researchers are alarmed that the decision seems to suggest

insights.claim: Preska noted 'without any hint of irony' that Rubio deemed it necessary to deport Ahmed in order to protect American freedom of expression and reject encroachments undermining free speech.
insights.speaker: Loretta Preska
insights.so_what: Judicial ridicule of the government's stated rationale in a published order is usable ammunition on appeal and signals weak substantive footing.
insights.locator: In that case, US District Judge Loretta Preska called out Rubio

insights.claim: Preska's order allowed the administration to begin removal proceedings after only five days, and Ahmed obtained an extended restraining order blocking detention or deportation until the appeals court rules.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: The five-day window shows how fast administrative action can follow a jurisdictional dismissal — procedural speed is itself a coercion tool.
insights.locator: For Ahmed, Preska's ruling came with high personal stakes.

insights.claim: Preska was bound by a recent ruling extending the government's removal authority to 'questions of law and fact' arising in challenges to removal, not just removal orders — but the full appeals court took the unusual step of granting rehearing en banc before any petition was filed, because six judges believed federal courts do have jurisdiction.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Sua sponte en banc rehearing is a strong tell that the controlling precedent will be overturned — the most concrete reason to expect the jurisdictional block to fall.
insights.quote: The full Court took the unusual step of granting rehearing en banc before a petition for rehearing was filed
insights.locator: But that recent ruling is currently being challenged

insights.claim: Ahmed narrowed his requested relief to disclaim any injunction preventing the government from commencing removal proceedings, seeking instead to resolve whether arrest and detention can be used to punish protected speech — a deliberate litigation strategy to escape the jurisdictional bar.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Separating retaliatory-detention claims from removal claims is the emerging template other targeted researchers will copy — watch whether courts accept the split.
insights.locator: To keep his fight alive, Ahmed reiterated to the appeals court

themes.theme: Musk, X, and the alleged retaliation motive

insights.claim: Ahmed says officials specifically cited his group's support for the European Union fining X a record $1 billion as the cause of his national-security designation.
insights.speaker: Imran Ahmed
insights.so_what: A direct link between an EU enforcement outcome and US immigration retaliation shows transatlantic platform regulation now carries personal legal risk for its evidence providers.
insights.locator: Ahmed told Ars that officials specifically cited his group's support

insights.claim: Ahmed alleges officials rely on 'shifting, contradictory, and unsupported rationales' and that no evidence has shown he poses 'serious adverse foreign policy consequences,' the statutory standard the State Department invokes.
insights.speaker: Imran Ahmed
insights.so_what: The elasticity of the 'serious adverse foreign policy consequences' standard is what makes the policy portable to other critics — it has no evidentiary floor.
insights.locator: However, so far, no evidence has shown that he might pose

insights.claim: Ahmed characterizes the action as the US government's power being used to silence someone who has annoyed a friend of the administration, naming Elon Musk directly.
insights.speaker: Imran Ahmed
insights.so_what: Alleged political-proximity capture of enforcement is a governance risk factor for any platform whose owner is close to the administration — including for advertisers and regulators abroad.
insights.quote: the use of the awe-inspiring power of the US government to silence someone who has annoyed a friend of the administration, Mr. Musk
insights.locator: Ahmed told Ars that he's willing to risk temporary detention

insights.claim: A State Department spokesperson declined to comment on the litigation but reiterated the department's authority to recommend removal proceedings for any noncitizen whose US activities could have serious adverse foreign policy consequences.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: The department restating the broad standard rather than defending the specific case indicates it intends to keep using the tool regardless of case outcomes.
insights.locator: Reached for comment on what risk Ahmed's ongoing research might pose

insights.claim: Ahmed argues the Department of Justice should be investigating a platform that is proliferating and creating child sex abuse material rather than punishing the person identifying the problem.
insights.speaker: Imran Ahmed
insights.so_what: The absence of a DOJ probe despite documented CSAM on X is itself a data point on selective enforcement — and a gap foreign regulators may fill instead.
insights.quote: I do think that DOJ should be focusing on a platform that is now proliferating and creating child sex abuse material rather than trying to punish the person who’s identifying the problem
insights.locator: And while the focus isn't completely on Musk

themes.theme: CSAM findings on X and Grok

insights.claim: A New York Times investigation using CCDH research found that some of the most egregious examples of child sexual abuse material continue to go undetected on X, with some images viewed hundreds of times.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Documented CSAM persistence is the single highest-severity content liability for a platform — it drives advertiser flight, app store risk and EU/UK enforcement.
insights.locator: CCDH contributed research to a major New York Times investigation

insights.claim: CCDH gave the Canadian Center for Children Protection access to more than four million links to Grok-generated images, and the review found 65 AI-generated CSAM images plus 75 known CSAM images.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: AI-generated CSAM emerging from a platform's own image model creates first-party liability rather than user-content liability — a materially worse legal posture.
insights.locator: CCDH gave access to more than four million links to Grok-generated images

insights.claim: X's only response to the CSAM findings was to link to an X Safety post stating the platform has zero tolerance for CSAM, offering no substantive rebuttal of the specific findings.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: A boilerplate response to documented failures is what regulators cite as evidence of inadequate systemic controls under the DSA and similar regimes.
insights.quote: X has zero tolerance for CSAM
insights.locator: (Asked for comment, X linked to an X Safety post

insights.claim: X has come under fire globally specifically because its chatbot Grok generated child sexual abuse material, moving the issue from moderation failure to model-safety failure.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Generative model outputs now sit inside the platform-liability perimeter — a precedent that raises compliance cost for every consumer AI image product.
insights.locator: when it comes to X—which has come under fire globally after its chatbot Grok generated CSAM

insights.claim: Ahmed says about 90 percent of CCDH's work is simply testing whether promised platform safeguards actually work, rather than making editorial judgments about speech.
insights.speaker: Imran Ahmed
insights.so_what: Safeguard verification is an auditable, falsifiable activity — it is also the exact function regulators will eventually mandate, making it a durable service category.
insights.locator: About 90 percent of that work is simply testing if promised safeguards actually work

insights.claim: CCDH is preparing a fall report on AI platform safety that Ahmed confirmed will show safeguards from firms including OpenAI are not working as they should.
insights.speaker: Imran Ahmed
insights.so_what: A pre-announced adverse finding on OpenAI safeguards is a datable headline risk for consumer AI firms this fall — watch for enterprise procurement and regulatory follow-on.
insights.locator: This fall, they're preparing a report on safety on AI platforms

insights.claim: Ahmed confirmed in his appeal that he will not leave the US or voluntarily submit to immigration detention, and will continue advocating for platform transparency under the immediate threat of arrest at any time.
insights.speaker: Ashley Belanger
insights.so_what: Refusal to self-deport forces the government to act visibly, converting a quiet chilling mechanism into a public test case with reputational cost.
insights.quote: does not intend to leave the United States or voluntarily submit to immigration detention while he seeks appellate review
insights.locator: In his appeal, he confirmed

insights.claim: Ahmed founded CCDH after losing a colleague to a gunman radicalized online, and after seven years of platform monitoring says he will take the fight to the Supreme Court if necessary.
insights.speaker: Imran Ahmed
insights.so_what: A founder motivated by personal loss and willing to escalate to the Supreme Court signals this case will not settle quietly — expect a multi-year legal overhang.
insights.quote: We have to show that we will not be cowed from this vital work, and it is vital
insights.locator: He said that he founded CCDH with the goal of making platforms safer

insights.claim: Ahmed frames the constitutional question as transparency not being censorship, arguing that speaking truth to the most powerful person on the planet is precisely the intention of the First Amendment.
insights.speaker: Imran Ahmed
insights.so_what: The transparency-versus-censorship framing is the rhetorical battleground that will determine whether platform research survives politically, not just legally.
insights.quote: I may be British, but even I know that transparency isn’t censorship and that speaking truth to the most powerful person on the planet is precisely the intention of the First Amendment
